---
title: "Querying ResStock with DuckDB"
subtitle: "A walkthrough for accessing the S3 bucket without downloading files"
---

[DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) can query Parquet files directly from S3 — no local download required. This walkthrough covers setup and a handful of useful starting queries against the `metadata_and_annual_results` table, which is the most common entry point for ResStock analysis.

::: {.callout-note}
All queries here run against OEDI's public S3 bucket, so no AWS credentials are needed. You do need an internet connection and `duckdb` installed (`pip install duckdb`).
:::

---

## Setup

```{python}
#| eval: false
import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()

con.execute("INSTALL httpfs;")
con.execute("LOAD httpfs;")
con.execute("SET s3_region = 'us-west-2';")
```

That's all the configuration needed. DuckDB's `httpfs` extension handles anonymous access to public S3 buckets automatically.

It helps to define the path to the metadata folder up front, since you'll reuse it across queries:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Root path — swap the filename to switch upgrade scenarios
METADATA = (
    "s3://oedi-data-lake/nrel-pds-building-stock/"
    "end-use-load-profiles-for-us-building-stock/2025/"
    "resstock_amy2018_release_1/metadata_and_annual_results/"
    "national/full/parquet/"
)

baseline    = METADATA + "upgrade0.parquet"
hp_upgrade  = METADATA + "upgrade4.parquet"   # Cold-climate ducted ASHP
```

---

## Explore the schema

Before writing queries it's useful to see what columns are available. The metadata files are wide (~hundreds of columns), so this gives you a lay of the land:

```{python}
#| eval: false
schema = con.execute(f"DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('{baseline}')").df()
print(schema[["column_name", "column_type"]].to_string(index=False))
```

A few column naming conventions to know:

- `in.*` — building input characteristics (e.g., `in.state`, `in.heating_fuel`, `in.vintage`)
- `out.*` — simulation outputs (e.g., `out.electricity.total.energy_consumption`)
- `weight` — the statistical weight for each sample (how many real U.S. homes it represents)
- `bldg_id` — unique building identifier, links to individual timeseries files

---

## Count buildings by state

A simple sanity check — how many simulated buildings are in each state? Multiplying by `weight` gives the estimated real housing units represented.

```{python}
#| eval: false
con.execute(f"""
    SELECT
        "in.state"                          AS state,
        COUNT(*)                            AS n_simulated,
        ROUND(SUM(weight))                  AS n_represented
    FROM read_parquet('{baseline}')
    GROUP BY "in.state"
    ORDER BY n_represented DESC
    LIMIT 10
""").df()
```

---

## Distribution of heating fuels

```{python}
#| eval: false
con.execute(f"""
    SELECT
        "in.heating_fuel"       AS heating_fuel,
        COUNT(*)                AS n_buildings,
        ROUND(SUM(weight))      AS housing_units_represented
    FROM read_parquet('{baseline}')
    GROUP BY "in.heating_fuel"
    ORDER BY housing_units_represented DESC
""").df()
```

---

## Compare annual electricity use: baseline vs. heat pump upgrade

Upgrade 4 applies a cold-climate ducted air source heat pump to all eligible buildings. This query pulls annual electricity consumption from both files and computes the difference — joining on `bldg_id` so each row is one building.

```{python}
#| eval: false
con.execute(f"""
    SELECT
        b.bldg_id,
        b."in.state"                                            AS state,
        b."in.heating_fuel"                                     AS baseline_fuel,
        b."out.electricity.total.energy_consumption"            AS elec_baseline_kwh,
        h."out.electricity.total.energy_consumption"            AS elec_hp_kwh,
        h."out.electricity.total.energy_consumption"
            - b."out.electricity.total.energy_consumption"      AS elec_delta_kwh
    FROM read_parquet('{baseline}')   AS b
    JOIN read_parquet('{hp_upgrade}') AS h USING (bldg_id)
    WHERE b."in.state" = 'CO'
    LIMIT 20
""").df()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
The `by_state` partition of the metadata is faster for single-state queries because DuckDB only reads the relevant partition. Swap the path like this:

```python
baseline_co = (
    "s3://oedi-data-lake/nrel-pds-building-stock/"
    "end-use-load-profiles-for-us-building-stock/2025/"
    "resstock_amy2018_release_1/metadata_and_annual_results/"
    "by_state/full/parquet/upgrade0.parquet"
)
```

The file structure is the same — Hive-partitioned by state — so tools that support partition pruning (DuckDB included) will only fetch the slices they need.
:::

---

## Reading a single building's timeseries

Once you've identified a building of interest from the metadata, you can pull its full sub-hourly timeseries. Files live at:

```
s3://oedi-data-lake/.../timeseries_individual_buildings/by_state/upgrade={N}/state={XX}/{bldg_id}-{N}.parquet
```

```{python}
#| eval: false
TIMESERIES_ROOT = (
    "s3://oedi-data-lake/nrel-pds-building-stock/"
    "end-use-load-profiles-for-us-building-stock/2025/"
    "resstock_amy2018_release_1/timeseries_individual_buildings/by_state/"
)

bldg_id  = 100102   # replace with a bldg_id from your metadata query
upgrade  = 0
state    = "AK"

ts_path = f"{TIMESERIES_ROOT}upgrade={upgrade}/state={state}/{bldg_id}-{upgrade}.parquet"

ts = con.execute(f"SELECT * FROM read_parquet('{ts_path}')").df()
print(ts.shape)      # should be ~35,040 rows (15-min intervals × 8,760 hours)
ts.head()
```

Each row is one 15-minute interval. Columns follow the same `out.*` naming convention as the metadata outputs, broken out by end use (e.g., `out.electricity.heating.energy_consumption`, `out.electricity.cooling.energy_consumption`).
